profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal brainstorming meeting in an ML research lab preparing a follow-up workshop submission and experimental plan around Perturbative Gradient Training (PGT). The team has already shown that PGT works on simulated dense and transformer-based models plus a magnonic auto-oscillation ring, and this meeting is focused on generating promising extension ideas that could make the next paper feel both methodologically stronger and more compelling to the physical computing community. The agenda is to brainstorm candidate directions for a 'next-step' study, quickly screen which ones are worth prototyping, and converge on 2-3 ideas to explore over the next month. The expected outcome is an informal shortlist of extension concepts, a rough sense of what would count as a convincing demonstration, and who will sketch the first experiments.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: approximate optimization, scientific ML, publication strategy for neuromorphic and physical ML systems
members.background: Lina leads a university-industry ML systems group and has recently been framing PGT as a general training principle for black-box dynamical modules embedded inside deep networks.
members.private_state: She wants brainstormed ideas that can support a broad methodological claim in the next paper without requiring a risky rebuild of the hardware setup, and she is especially concerned with making the work read as more than a one-off hardware demonstration.
hidden_assumptions: A 'physical reservoir result' can be supported by using the same magnonic device but varying software-side training structure around it, without needing extensive new hardware operating regimes.
Calling a direction 'scalable' mainly means the optimization signal remains usable as model width, sequence length, or layer count grows in simulation, even if hardware throughput is unchanged.
A 'strong baseline' means comparison to standard gradient-based training on a matched simulated architecture to show that PGT is not giving up too much accuracy.

When discussing 'the transformer setup,' she means the previously used transformer with a single reservoir block inserted into the sequence model, not a substantially reconfigured hybrid architecture.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Research Scientist for Experimental Reservoir Systems
members.expertise: physical reservoir computing, magnonic devices, measurement pipelines, hardware-in-the-loop optimization
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's magnonic auto-oscillation ring platform and translated the original PGT idea into the hardware experiment by stabilizing repeated forward passes under noisy lab conditions.
members.private_state: He wants the next project to foreground genuinely hardware-native benefits and avoid claims that look broad on paper but are mostly simulation extensions; he is also trying to avoid any plan that quietly assumes much more device stability or lab time than is realistic.
hidden_assumptions: A 'physical reservoir result' should involve the hardware operating in a substantively new way or under a more realistic hardware-in-the-loop training condition, not just another software wrapper around the same measurements.
Calling something 'scalable' mainly refers to whether the perturbation-and-measurement procedure keeps wall-clock and measurement burden manageable on real hardware.
A 'strong baseline' means other gradient-free or hardware-compatible estimators such as SPSA, node perturbation, or finite-difference variants under the same noisy measurement budget.

When discussing 'the transformer setup,' he thinks of the hardware-inspired sequence experiment where the reservoir processes temporal inputs and the surrounding network is minimal, because that is the practically reproducible version in the lab.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a physical reservoir paper
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss making the next study 'more physical' or having a 'real physical reservoir result.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this can be achieved by centering the magnonic reservoir in the narrative while expanding the surrounding simulated architecture and analysis, even if the hardware portion itself changes only modestly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this requires a materially new hardware experiment or a more demanding hardware-in-the-loop protocol, otherwise it is still mostly a simulation paper with a token device section.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both value physical relevance and use the same praise words ('more physical,' 'real hardware story'), so the divergence hides inside their unstated standard for what qualifies.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say an idea should test whether PGT 'scales.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means algorithmic scalability: whether perturbative gradient estimates remain effective as network size, sequence length, and depth increase in larger simulated models.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means experimental scalability: whether the number of perturbation shots, repeated measurements, and calibration overhead stay feasible on the magnonic platform.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research meetings, 'scales' is a routine positive term, so each hears their preferred interpretation and sees no need to unpack it unless implementation planning gets very concrete.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need a 'strong baseline' to make the brainstorming shortlist credible.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is mentally referring to the backprop-trained simulated dense/transformer variants already used in the prior paper lineage as the obvious gold-standard baseline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally referring to hardware-compatible black-box optimizers like SPSA and finite-difference perturbation methods run under the same forward-pass budget and device noise conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'strong baseline' is standard and sounds settled; both assume there is an obvious comparison family, but the 'obvious' referent differs by community lens rather than explicit disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the transformer follow-up
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss extending the 'transformer setup' as a candidate next experiment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes larger sequence tasks, more layers around the reservoir block, and ablations on where the reservoir is inserted in an otherwise standard transformer pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this only includes the narrow, hardware-reproducible sequence-processing wrapper already used around the reservoir, not a broader transformer architecture search.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are reusing the same label from earlier work, the boundary of what belongs to that setup feels shared and pre-established, even though each has abstracted a different version from the prior project.

turns.inner_thought: I need options that strengthen the next paper's methodological arc without committing us to a fragile new hardware campaign. If we can keep the same magnonic device central in the story but vary the training structure and analyses around it, that is enough to make this feel more physical for the workshop. The key is to avoid another result that reads like an isolated demo.
turns.utterance: Okay, maybe we can use this meeting just to generate a clean shortlist. What I want is a follow-up that makes PGT feel more substantial, a bit more physical, and still feasible on this cycle.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but 'more physical' only really lands if the hardware is doing something meaningfully new or at least the hardware-in-the-loop protocol is tougher and more realistic. Also, if we say something scales, I want that to mean we can actually run it on the ring without exploding the number of shots, reruns, and calibration steps.
turns.utterance: I agree. The strongest options are probably the ones that show the method scales and still look believable on the magnonic platform.

turns.inner_thought: A natural next step is the transformer setup from the earlier work, but pushed to longer-context tasks, deeper surrounding layers, and maybe different insertion points for the reservoir block. That would let us test whether PGT's signal still behaves as sequence length and model depth grow, which is exactly the kind of scaling story I want.
turns.utterance: One obvious direction is to extend the transformer setup to a longer-context sequence task and see whether PGT still behaves well when the surrounding model gets deeper.

turns.inner_thought: That could work if 'transformer setup' means the lean sequence wrapper we already know how to reproduce around the device. I definitely do not want this to turn into a big architecture expansion. The attraction is that we might keep the hardware in the loop and avoid rebuilding the device side, while still collecting a genuinely physical result.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I think the transformer setup is attractive for exactly that reason. It could let us keep the hardware in the loop without rebuilding the device side too much.

turns.inner_thought: Whatever we do, reviewers will want the obvious comparison: standard gradient-based training on the matched simulated architecture. If PGT stays reasonably close there, the broader claim survives. I should flag baseline expectations early so the shortlist doesn't drift into something that's impossible to position.
turns.utterance: Whichever direction we choose, we'll need a strong baseline so reviewers can immediately see that PGT remains competitive.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely, but the baseline has to be fair under the same hardware realities. For me that means other hardware-compatible perturbation estimators under the same forward-pass budget and repeat conditions, not some idealized training loop that ignores lab noise and measurement cost.
turns.utterance: Definitely. It would be great if the strong baseline uses the same perturbation budget and repeated forward-pass conditions as the hardware runs.

turns.inner_thought: A second angle is to explicitly frame PGT as a general scalable training primitive for black-box modules. We can do the width and insertion-depth sweeps in simulation, maybe over larger sequence models, and then anchor the whole thing with one hardware result from the magnonic reservoir. That gives us breadth without needing the lab to support every claim experimentally.
turns.utterance: A second idea is to frame PGT as a scalable training primitive for black-box modules: sweep model width and reservoir insertion depth, then anchor it with one hardware result.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that if we keep it physical in a way that matters on the device. A useful addition would be to probe whether the ring tolerates a wider perturbation schedule without forcing endless reruns or restabilization. That would say something concrete about whether the procedure scales experimentally.
turns.utterance: I like that framing. And if we keep it physical, we could also test whether the device tolerates a broader perturbation schedule without excessive reruns.

turns.inner_thought: A robustness angle could be very publishable: show PGT against the usual baseline under drift and noise, and argue it's well suited when clean backprop isn't available through the module. That would help position this as a general principle rather than just a magnonics curiosity.
turns.utterance: A third option is a robustness-focused study: compare PGT against the usual baseline under drift and noise, and argue it's especially suitable when backprop is impractical.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, robustness is probably one of the best hardware stories we can tell, but only if the comparator is a fair hardware-side one. Reviewers in this area will care whether we compared against methods they'd actually consider running with noisy repeated measurements, not an idealized software reference.
turns.utterance: I think robustness could read really well, especially if the baseline is something reviewers recognize as a fair hardware-side comparator rather than an idealized training loop.

turns.inner_thought: Given time, the best pair is probably the transformer extension plus robustness. Together they can show PGT scales in the larger-model sense and give us a cleaner physical reservoir story, while still letting the hardware result serve as the anchor instead of the whole contribution.
turns.utterance: If I had to narrow it now, I'd keep the transformer extension and the robustness study. Together those should show PGT scales and give us a cleaner physical reservoir story.

turns.inner_thought: That split makes sense. I'll sketch the hardware-in-the-loop version of the sequence experiment I know we can actually run, plus fair baseline comparisons under the same measurement budget. Lina can shape the larger paper narrative around that. Hopefully the scope stays grounded once we start writing.
